properties.title: Villa's zone at its peak (late 1914)
properties.label: Villa
properties.description: After the Constitutionalist split in autumn 1914, Pancho Villa's División del Norte held Chihuahua, Durango, the cotton district of La Laguna, Zacatecas and Aguascalientes, and the Central railway south through the Bajío to Mexico City. The north's cattle, cotton and mines, sold across the US border, paid for arms. Villa's power ran along the railways, and he never held a Gulf port or the oil zone that sustained Carranza.
properties.note: Hand-drawn, then clipped to modern Mexico so that it stops at the Rio Grande and the border. It shows the core that Katz describes for December 1914, not a front line: control in the Sierra Madre and the deserts was thin, and the edges in Coahuila and the Bajío moved from week to week. Conventionist allies outside the core (José María Maytorena in Sonora, the Conventionist hold on San Luis Potosí, and Guadalajara, taken in December 1914 and fought over into 1915) are not included.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Robert E. Quirk, The Mexican Revolution, 1914–1915: The Convention of Aguascalientes (Indiana University Press, 1960).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Zapatista zone (1914–1915)
properties.label: Zapata
properties.description: Zapata's Liberation Army of the South held Morelos and the adjacent districts of Puebla, Guerrero, the State of México and the southern Federal District. It was a movement of village communities fighting for the land that the sugar haciendas had taken, under the Plan of Ayala. With Mexico City in Conventionist hands in 1915 its chiefs carried out a land reform in Morelos, run from Zapata's headquarters at Tlaltizapán.
properties.note: Hand-drawn from Womack's account and anchored on Milpa Alta, Amecameca, Atlixco, Izúcar de Matamoros, Chiautla, Iguala, Taxco and Tenancingo. Zapatista bands also operated in Guerrero beyond Iguala (Chilpancingo fell to them in March 1914) and in southern Puebla; their reach outside Morelos varied with the season and the campaign.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 14–15.

properties.title: Carranza's Constitutionalist zone (December 1914)
properties.label: Carranza
properties.description: When the Convention and Carranza broke in November 1914, Carranza withdrew to Veracruz and held the Gulf coast from the lower Rio Grande to Yucatán, with the northeast around Monterrey and Saltillo, Chiapas, and a foothold on the Sonora border at Agua Prieta and Naco. The zone looked small on a map, but it had the customs revenue of Veracruz and Tampico, the oil taxes and the henequen of Yucatán, and so the money to buy arms. From there Obregón opened the campaign that retook Puebla and Mexico City in January 1915.
properties.note: Hand-drawn, then clipped to modern Mexico, so the northern and southern edges follow the modern US, Guatemala and Belize borders; the western edge is a loose line along the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Puebla–Veracruz border, with the front facing the Villistas at El Ébano, near Tampico. Felipe Ángeles took Saltillo and Monterrey for Villa in January 1915. Oaxaca, which declared itself sovereign under local leaders, Carrancista and other forces in Jalisco, Michoacán and Sinaloa, and the "Mapache" rebellion of Chiapas planters against the Carrancista governor are not shown separately.

sources.citation: Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Charles C. Cumberland, Mexican Revolution: The Constitutionalist Years (University of Texas Press, 1972).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Aquiles Serdán's house besieged in Puebla
properties.label: Serdán, Puebla
properties.description: Madero's Plan of San Luis Potosí called for a national rising on 20 November 1910 against Porfirio Díaz's re-election. Two days early, police and troops attacked the Puebla house of the Maderista organiser Aquiles Serdán; his brother Máximo was killed in the shooting, and Aquiles, found hiding in the house, was shot, by most accounts the next morning. The rising in the cities failed, and the revolution survived in the mountains of western Chihuahua under Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa.
properties.note: The house, at 6 Oriente 206 in the historic centre of Puebla, is now the Museo Regional de la Revolución Mexicana. The Plan of San Luis Potosí itself is mapped in the Porfiriato era.

sources.citation: Stanley R. Ross, Francisco I. Madero: Apostle of Mexican Democracy (Columbia University Press, 1955).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Toribio Ortega rises at Cuchillo Parado
properties.label: Cuchillo Parado
properties.description: Six days before the date set by Madero, Toribio Ortega, head of the Anti-Reelectionist club of Cuchillo Parado, a village near the Conchos river in northeastern Chihuahua that had been fighting a local cacique over its lands, took up arms with a few dozen men on learning that troops were coming to arrest him. Similar village risings spread through Chihuahua over the following week, and by December the rebels held much of the sierra. Ortega later commanded a brigade of Villa's División del Norte and died of typhoid in 1914.
properties.note: Marked at the village of Cuchillo Parado (municipality of Coyame del Sotol). Ortega's own account gives about sixty men, others about seventy. Whether this was the first rising of the Revolution is disputed locally with Pascual Orozco's rising at San Isidro (19 November).

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Wikipedia (es), "Toribio Ortega Ramírez".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Magonista rising in Baja California
properties.label: Magonistas 1911
properties.description: Followers of Ricardo Flores Magón's Liberal Party took Mexicali on 29 January 1911 and, with a mixed force that included American IWW members and adventurers, Tijuana in May. The anarchists were never part of Madero's movement, and the presence of filibusters let their enemies paint the rising as an attempt to annex the peninsula. Federal troops under Celso Vega retook Tijuana on 22 June and the rising collapsed.
properties.note: Marked at Mexicali, the first town taken; Tijuana, about 170 km to the west, is not marked separately. The rebels also fought at Tecate and El Álamo.

sources.citation: Lowell L. Blaisdell, The Desert Revolution: Baja California, 1911 (University of Wisconsin Press, 1962).
Wikipedia, "Magonista rebellion of 1911".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Revolutionaries take Ciudad Juárez
properties.label: Ciudad Juárez 1911
properties.description: Against Madero's orders, Orozco and Villa attacked the federal garrison of Ciudad Juárez, across the river from El Paso, and General Juan Navarro surrendered on 10 May. It was the first major city taken by the rebels, and it gave Madero a port of entry on the US border. Díaz, facing risings across the country, came to terms within two weeks.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the fighting moved through the streets from the rebel camps west and south of town.

sources.citation: Stanley R. Ross, Francisco I. Madero: Apostle of Mexican Democracy (Columbia University Press, 1955).
Michael C. Meyer, Mexican Rebel: Pascual Orozco and the Mexican Revolution, 1910–1915 (University of Nebraska Press, 1967).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Zapatistas take Cuautla
properties.label: Cuautla 1911
properties.description: The Maderista revolutionaries of Morelos, led by Emiliano Zapata, besieged Cuautla, the sugar town in the east of the state, held by the federal Fifth Cavalry Regiment. After six days of heavy fighting in the town, the federals withdrew on 19 May. Coming just after the fall of Ciudad Juárez, it added to the pressure on Díaz, who resigned a week later, and it made Zapata the leading revolutionary chief in the south.
properties.note: Marked at the main square of Cuautla; the fighting spread through the town.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Treaty of Ciudad Juárez
properties.label: Treaty of Ciudad Juárez
properties.description: Representatives of Díaz and Madero signed an agreement under which Díaz and Vice President Corral would resign and Foreign Minister Francisco León de la Barra would serve as interim president until elections. Díaz resigned on 25 May and sailed for Europe from Veracruz. The treaty left the federal army and the Porfirian state in place, which many revolutionaries, Zapata among them, came to see as Madero's fatal mistake.
properties.note: Marked at the former customs house (now the Museo de la Revolución en la Frontera), where the treaty was signed at night.
properties.modern_place: Museo de la Revolución en la Frontera, Ciudad Juárez

sources.citation: Stanley R. Ross, Francisco I. Madero: Apostle of Mexican Democracy (Columbia University Press, 1955).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Plan of Ayala
properties.label: Plan of Ayala
properties.description: Zapata and the chiefs of the Morelos revolution, breaking with President Madero, proclaimed their own plan in the mountains of southwestern Puebla, where they had taken refuge from federal campaigns. It declared Madero a traitor and demanded the return of lands, woods and waters taken by the haciendas, the expropriation, with compensation, of a third of the great estates, and the confiscation of the property of those who opposed it. It remained the Zapatista programme for the rest of the decade.
properties.note: Marked at Ayoxuxtla (Ayoxustla), Huehuetlán el Chico, Puebla, where the plan was signed and proclaimed; it bears the name of Villa de Ayala, Morelos, the movement's birthplace.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Plan de Ayala, 28 November 1911 (published in Diario del Hogar, Mexico City, 15 December 1911).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Orozco rebels against Madero
properties.label: Orozco's revolt
properties.description: Pascual Orozco, the leading general of 1910–11, broke with Madero in early March 1912 and issued his own programme, the Plan Orozquista (or Plan de la Empacadora), at Chihuahua City on 25 March. Backed at first by the Chihuahua oligarchy around the Terrazas–Creel family, his rebellion held most of the state until federal forces under Victoriano Huerta drove it back that summer, raising Huerta to prominence.
properties.note: Marked at Chihuahua City, where the plan was signed in the building of a meat-packing plant (empacadora).

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, Mexican Rebel: Pascual Orozco and the Mexican Revolution, 1910–1915 (University of Nebraska Press, 1967).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Battles of Rellano
properties.label: Rellano 1912
properties.description: Fighting along the Central railway south of Jiménez decided Orozco's rebellion. In the first battle (late March 1912) the Orozquistas routed a federal army under the Minister of War, José González Salas, who took his own life. In the second (22–23 May) a federal division under Victoriano Huerta defeated Orozco; he was beaten again at Bachimba in July, and his movement broke up into guerrilla bands.
properties.note: Marked at the Rellano railway station; the fighting stretched along the line. Sources give 23 or 24 March for the first battle, so only the month is shown for the start.

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, Mexican Rebel: Pascual Orozco and the Mexican Revolution, 1910–1915 (University of Nebraska Press, 1967).
Michael C. Meyer, Huerta: A Political Portrait (University of Nebraska Press, 1972).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Félix Díaz rises at Veracruz
properties.label: Félix Díaz 1912
properties.description: Porfirio Díaz's nephew Félix seized the port of Veracruz with part of its garrison and called for Madero's overthrow, but no other units joined him, and federal forces under General Joaquín Beltrán retook the city a week later. Condemned to death, he was saved by a court stay and imprisoned in Mexico City, from where he was freed to lead the coup of February 1913.
properties.note: Marked at the port. Gillingham (ch. 14) has him held in the Santiago Tlatelolco military prison; most accounts put him in the Penitentiary (Lecumberri) and Bernardo Reyes in Santiago Tlatelolco. Both were freed on 9 February 1913.

sources.citation: Peter V. N. Henderson, Félix Díaz, the Porfirians, and the Mexican Revolution (University of Nebraska Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Decena Trágica
properties.label: Decena Trágica
properties.description: Generals Bernardo Reyes and Félix Díaz rose against Madero in Mexico City; Reyes was killed attacking the National Palace and Díaz shut himself in the Ciudadela arsenal. For ten days the rebels and government forces under Victoriano Huerta shelled each other across the city centre, killing many civilians, while Huerta negotiated with the rebels and the US ambassador, Henry Lane Wilson. On 18 February Huerta had Madero and Vice President Pino Suárez arrested and agreed with Félix Díaz, in the "Pact of the Embassy", to take power.
properties.note: Marked at the Ciudadela, now the Biblioteca de México. The fighting covered much of the centre between the Ciudadela and the National Palace.

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, Huerta: A Political Portrait (University of Nebraska Press, 1972).
Friedrich Katz, The Secret War in Mexico: Europe, the United States and the Mexican Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Madero and Pino Suárez murdered
properties.label: Madero murdered
properties.description: After resigning under duress on 19 February, Madero and Pino Suárez were held in the National Palace. On the night of 22 February they were taken out, supposedly for transfer to the federal penitentiary of Lecumberri, and shot beside it; the official story was that they were killed in a rescue attempt. Huerta, made president by Congress, faced risings in Coahuila, Sonora, Chihuahua and Morelos within weeks.
properties.note: Marked at the former Lecumberri penitentiary, now the Archivo General de la Nación; the killings took place outside its walls.
properties.modern_place: Archivo General de la Nación, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Michael C. Meyer, Huerta: A Political Portrait (University of Nebraska Press, 1972).
Stanley R. Ross, Francisco I. Madero: Apostle of Mexican Democracy (Columbia University Press, 1955).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 14.

properties.title: Plan of Guadalupe
properties.label: Plan of Guadalupe
properties.description: Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, refused to recognise Huerta, and at the Hacienda de Guadalupe officers of his small force signed a plan naming him First Chief of the Constitutionalist Army. It was purely political: it promised to restore constitutional government but said nothing about land. Movements in Sonora and Chihuahua joined under it, and after defeats in Coahuila Carranza moved his headquarters to Sonora later in 1913.
properties.note: Marked at the ex-hacienda of Guadalupe (now a historic site), in the north of the municipality of Ramos Arizpe, about 100 km from Saltillo by the Monclova highway.
properties.modern_place: Hacienda de Guadalupe, Ramos Arizpe, Coahuila

sources.citation: Plan de Guadalupe, signed at the Hacienda de Guadalupe, Coahuila, 26 March 1913.
Charles C. Cumberland, Mexican Revolution: The Constitutionalist Years (University of Texas Press, 1972).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: The División del Norte down the Central railway
properties.label: División del Norte 1913–14
properties.description: Villa's army moved by train along the Mexican Central railway, the line that ran from El Paso to Mexico City. It took Ciudad Juárez by surprise with a captured coal train in November 1913, beat the federals at Tierra Blanca and occupied Chihuahua, then in March 1914 came south through Jiménez and Escalón to La Laguna. After Torreón it turned to Zacatecas, the gateway to central Mexico, and destroyed the federal army there in June.
properties.note: Main stops only, along the railway. The detour east to Paredón and Saltillo in May 1914 and the Ojinaga campaign of January 1914 are not drawn. Between Torreón and Fresnillo the line is straightened.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Villa takes Torreón
properties.label: Torreón 1914
properties.description: Torreón, the railway junction and centre of the La Laguna cotton district, was the key to north-central Mexico. Villa attacked through Gómez Palacio and Lerdo from late March, and after more than a week of heavy fighting the federal commander José Refugio Velasco evacuated the city on the night of 2 April; his army was beaten again at San Pedro de las Colonias. Villa had also held Torreón briefly in October 1913.
properties.note: Marked at Torreón; much of the fighting was on the hills around Gómez Palacio (Cerro de la Pila) and Torreón. Accounts date the opening of the attack (at Sacramento and Gómez Palacio) between 21 and 23 March, so only the month is shown for the start; the federals left the city on 2 April and Villa occupied it on the 3rd.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Michael C. Meyer, Huerta: A Political Portrait (University of Nebraska Press, 1972).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Tampico incident
properties.label: Tampico incident
properties.description: Federal troops in Tampico, then besieged by Constitutionalists, briefly arrested US sailors who had landed from a whaleboat near a bridge. Though they were released with an apology, Admiral Henry T. Mayo demanded a 21-gun salute to the US flag, and President Wilson, who refused to recognise Huerta, used the refusal as grounds for intervention.

sources.citation: Robert E. Quirk, An Affair of Honor: Woodrow Wilson and the Occupation of Veracruz (University of Kentucky Press, 1962).
Friedrich Katz, The Secret War in Mexico: Europe, the United States and the Mexican Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1981).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: US occupation of Veracruz
properties.label: Veracruz 1914
properties.description: To stop a German ship, the Ypiranga, from landing arms for Huerta, US sailors and marines seized the port of Veracruz. Cadets of the Naval School and townspeople resisted; nineteen Americans and many more Mexicans were killed. The occupation cut Huerta off from his main customs house, but it was condemned by Carranza as well. US forces left in November 1914, leaving the port to Carranza.

sources.citation: Robert E. Quirk, An Affair of Honor: Woodrow Wilson and the Occupation of Veracruz (University of Kentucky Press, 1962).
Friedrich Katz, The Secret War in Mexico: Europe, the United States and the Mexican Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1981).
John Mason Hart, Empire and Revolution: The Americans in Mexico since the Civil War (University of California Press, 2002).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Battle of Zacatecas
properties.label: Zacatecas 1914
properties.description: Defying Carranza, who wanted to keep him in the north, Villa attacked Zacatecas, the silver city that commanded the railway to Aguascalientes and the centre. The División del Norte stormed the hills around the town, including La Bufa and El Grillo, and destroyed the federal garrison as it fled, in one of the bloodiest battles of the revolution. It finished Huerta's army, but Carranza then cut off Villa's coal supply, and Obregón reached Mexico City first.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the battle was fought on the hills immediately around it.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Obregón's campaign down the west coast
properties.label: Obregón 1913–14
properties.description: Álvaro Obregón, commanding the Sonoran forces, cleared the federals from the border towns (Nogales, Cananea, Naco) in spring 1913 and defeated them near Guaymas at Santa Rosa and Santa María. Leaving Guaymas and Mazatlán besieged, he moved down the Pacific coast along the Southern Pacific of Mexico railway, took Culiacán (November 1913) and Tepic (May 1914), and routed the federals at Orendáin before entering Guadalajara on 8 July 1914. He then marched through the Bajío and Querétaro and entered Mexico City on 15 August.
properties.note: Main stops only. The line starts at Nogales after the border campaign; the march from Tepic across the Barranca to Guadalajara and the stages through the Bajío are straightened.

sources.citation: Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Treaties of Teoloyucan
properties.label: Teoloyucan
properties.description: Huerta had resigned on 15 July 1914 and gone into exile through Puerto México (Coatzacoalcos). At Teoloyucan, north of the capital, Obregón and representatives of the interim government agreed the surrender of Mexico City and the dissolution of the federal army, which was to withdraw and disband. Unlike in 1911, the old army ceased to exist.

sources.citation: Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Michael C. Meyer, Huerta: A Political Portrait (University of Nebraska Press, 1972).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Convention of Aguascalientes
properties.label: Aguascalientes Convention
properties.description: To settle the quarrel between Carranza and Villa, revolutionary generals met first in Mexico City and then, from 10 October 1914, in the neutral city of Aguascalientes, where Zapatista delegates joined them and the convention adopted the principles of the Plan of Ayala. It declared itself sovereign, elected Eulalio Gutiérrez provisional president in early November, and demanded that Carranza step down. Carranza refused, and Obregón and most of the Constitutionalist generals sided with him, leaving the Convention to Villa and Zapata.
properties.note: The delegates sat in the Teatro Morelos.

sources.citation: Robert E. Quirk, The Mexican Revolution, 1914–1915: The Convention of Aguascalientes (Indiana University Press, 1960).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Carranza's government at Veracruz
properties.label: Carranza at Veracruz
properties.description: After the US evacuation, Carranza made Veracruz his capital. To win support against Villa and Zapata he issued social reforms there: additions to the Plan of Guadalupe (12 December 1914), an agrarian law (6 January 1915) promising the restoration of village lands, and a pact with the Casa del Obrero Mundial (February 1915), whose "Red Battalions" fought for Obregón. The port's customs and the Tampico oil taxes paid for the war.
properties.note: Marked at the port. Veracruz served as the seat of Carranza's government for about eleven months, until October 1915 (Ulloa); the exact day of departure is not given.

sources.citation: Berta Ulloa, Veracruz, capital de la nación (1914–1915) (El Colegio de México, 1986).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
John Mason Hart, Revolutionary Mexico: The Coming and Process of the Mexican Revolution (University of California Press, 1987).
Charles C. Cumberland, Mexican Revolution: The Constitutionalist Years (University of Texas Press, 1972).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Manuel Peláez and the oil zone
properties.label: Peláez
properties.description: Manuel Peláez, from a landowning family of the Huasteca that had leased land to the oil companies, rose against Carranza and held the countryside of the Golden Lane fields of northern Veracruz for most of the decade. The companies paid him to protect their wells and pipelines, and five Carrancista campaigns in 1917–18 failed to dislodge him, so that Mexico's richest export zone stayed outside the government's control. He joined Obregón in 1920.
properties.note: Marked at Temapache (Álamo Temapache), where in December 1914 Peláez ordered the companies to pay their taxes; his forces ranged over the oil country between Tuxpan and Tampico. The start is when he began levying the companies, and the end when he backed the Plan of Agua Prieta. Gillingham (ch. 15) gives the payments as $25,000 a month.

sources.citation: Jonathan C. Brown, Oil and Revolution in Mexico (University of California Press, 1993).
Wikipedia, "Manuel Peláez".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Villa and Zapata meet at Xochimilco
properties.label: Pact of Xochimilco
properties.description: Villa and Zapata met for the first time at Xochimilco, south of the capital, and agreed to an alliance against Carranza: Villa accepted the Plan of Ayala, and the two armies divided the campaign, Villa taking the north and Zapata the east toward Puebla and Veracruz. Their alliance never became a joint strategy.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).

properties.title: Villa and Zapata in Mexico City
properties.label: Mexico City Dec 1914
properties.description: The armies of the North and the South paraded through Mexico City, and Villa and Zapata were photographed in the National Palace, Villa in the presidential chair. It was the high point of the popular revolution. Within weeks Zapata had gone back to Morelos and Villa to the north, and in January 1915 the Convention government abandoned the capital as Obregón advanced from Puebla.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Robert E. Quirk, The Mexican Revolution, 1914–1915: The Convention of Aguascalientes (Indiana University Press, 1960).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Siege of El Ébano
properties.label: El Ébano 1915
properties.description: Villista forces coming down from San Luis Potosí attacked the Carrancista lines at El Ébano, on the railway to Tampico, for more than two months. Holding the line protected Tampico and the oil fields, whose taxes funded Carranza; the Carrancistas fought from trenches with machine guns and armoured trains in one of the longest battles of the revolution.
properties.note: Marked at Ébano, San Luis Potosí; the lines ran across the railway nearby. Sources give 21 or 28 March for the start, so only the month is shown.

sources.citation: Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Jonathan C. Brown, Oil and Revolution in Mexico (University of California Press, 1993).

properties.title: Battles of Celaya
properties.label: Celaya 1915
properties.description: In the Bajío, on the railway between Querétaro and Irapuato, Obregón dug in at Celaya behind trenches, barbed wire and machine guns, and let Villa's cavalry wear itself out in frontal charges (6–7 April). Villa attacked again on 13–15 April and was routed when Obregón's reserve cavalry struck his flanks. The two battles broke the División del Norte's offensive power and turned the war in Carranza's favour.
properties.note: Marked at the city; the lines lay on its outskirts and across the plain to the west.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Battle of Trinidad (León)
properties.label: Trinidad 1915
properties.description: After Celaya the armies met again west of León, around Trinidad station and the hacienda of Santa Ana del Conde, in some five weeks of fighting from late April to early June 1915. Obregón lost his right arm to a shell at Santa Ana del Conde but won the battle; Villa retreated north, was beaten again at Aguascalientes in July, and lost the centre of the country.
properties.note: Marked at Santa Ana del Conde (municipality of León); the fighting extended along the railway between León and Silao. Exact dates differ between sources, so only months are shown. Gillingham (ch. 15) calls it the Battle of León and dates the decisive day to 3 June 1915, when Obregón lost his arm and Benjamín Hill led the counterattack.
properties.modern_place: Santa Ana del Conde, León, Guanajuato

sources.citation: Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Salvador Alvarado takes Yucatán
properties.label: Alvarado in Mérida
properties.description: Carranza sent General Salvador Alvarado to put down a revolt by Abel Ortiz Argumedo, backed by the henequen planters. Alvarado entered Mérida on 19 March 1915 and governed until 1918, enforcing the end of debt servitude on the estates and using the state henequen marketing commission to capture the profits of the fibre, which was in high wartime demand in the United States, for the Constitutionalist treasury.

sources.citation: Gilbert M. Joseph, Revolution from Without: Yucatán, Mexico, and the United States, 1880–1924 (Cambridge University Press, 1982).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).

properties.title: Villa repulsed at Agua Prieta
properties.label: Agua Prieta 1915
properties.description: Villa marched his remaining army across the Sierra Madre into Sonora and attacked Agua Prieta, on the Arizona border, at the beginning of November 1915. Plutarco Elías Calles's garrison, reinforced by Carrancista troops whom the US government, having recognised Carranza on 19 October, allowed to travel by rail through US territory, beat him off. Villa, believing he had been betrayed by Washington, turned against the United States.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Friedrich Katz, The Secret War in Mexico: Europe, the United States and the Mexican Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1981).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Esteban Cantú's Baja California
properties.label: Cantú
properties.description: Colonel Esteban Cantú, military commander at Mexicali, made himself governor of the Northern District of Baja California in January 1915 and ran it almost independently of the warring factions, cut off from the rest of Mexico except by sea and through the United States. He moved the capital from Ensenada to Mexicali, the centre of the booming cotton valley, and paid for streets, water, lighting and the first road linking Mexicali, Tecate, Tijuana and Ensenada with taxes on cotton, gambling, saloons and the opium trade run by Mexicali's Chinese merchants. He gave up power in August 1920 when the new Sonoran government sent forces against him.
properties.note: Marked at Mexicali, which became the district capital on 20 November 1915. The opium taxes are from Gillingham (ch. 21) and a Mexican study found by search; the Spanish Wikipedia article speaks only of gambling and vice.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (es), "Esteban Cantú Jiménez".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 21.

properties.title: First Feminist Congress, Mérida
properties.label: Feminist Congress
properties.description: Governor Salvador Alvarado convened in Mérida the first feminist congress in Mexico, attended by about 600 women, most of them schoolteachers. It debated secular education, women's work and, in its most radical motions, the vote; a second congress followed later in 1916. It made Yucatán an early centre of revolutionary feminism, though women did not get the national vote until the 1950s.
properties.note: Marked at the Teatro Peón Contreras, where the congress met. Attendance is given as 600 to 700.

sources.citation: Anna Macías, Against All Odds: The Feminist Movement in Mexico to 1940 (Greenwood Press, 1982).
Wikipedia, "First Feminist Congress of Yucatán".
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 16.

properties.title: Villa's raid on Columbus
properties.label: Columbus raid
properties.description: Before dawn several hundred Villistas attacked the border town of Columbus, New Mexico, and the US cavalry post of Camp Furlong beside it, burning part of the town and killing about eighteen American soldiers and civilians before being driven back with heavy losses. Katz argues that Villa believed Carranza had sold Mexico to the United States and hoped to provoke an intervention that would discredit him.
properties.note: Marked at Columbus; Camp Furlong was on the south side of town (now Pancho Villa State Park). Gillingham (ch. 15) dates the raid to 8 March 1916 (the Villistas crossed the border that night and attacked before dawn on the 9th), places Columbus on the Arizona border (it is in New Mexico) and gives seventeen Americans killed.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, "Pancho Villa and the Attack on Columbus, New Mexico," American Historical Review 83, no. 1 (1978): 101–130.
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Clarence C. Clendenen, Blood on the Border: The United States Army and the Mexican Irregulars (Macmillan, 1969).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: The Punitive Expedition
properties.label: Punitive Expedition
properties.description: General John J. Pershing led about 10,000 US troops into Chihuahua to capture Villa. From the main base at Colonia Dublán, a Mormon colony, cavalry columns pushed south through Namiquipa, San Antonio de los Arenales and Satevó to Parral, some 500 miles from Columbus by the expedition's route, without catching him. After clashes with Carrancista troops at Parral and Carrizal the expedition fell back to Colonia Dublán, and it left Mexico in February 1917, as the US prepared to enter the European war.
properties.note: One representative line through documented stops (Columbus, Palomas, Colonia Dublán, Namiquipa, San Antonio de los Arenales, Satevó, Parral). The expedition moved in several columns across a wide area of western Chihuahua, including a second column from Culberson's Ranch and the fight at Guerrero (29 March 1916), which are not drawn. Gillingham (ch. 15) gives 5,000 men at the start and 11,000 at the peak, and Parral as more than 400 miles south of the border.

sources.citation: Clarence C. Clendenen, Blood on the Border: The United States Army and the Mexican Irregulars (Macmillan, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Friedrich Katz, The Secret War in Mexico: Europe, the United States and the Mexican Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1981).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Clash at Parral
properties.label: Parral 1916
properties.description: A US cavalry squadron under Major Frank Tompkins rode into Parral, the farthest point the expedition reached, and was driven out by townspeople and the Carrancista garrison, retreating north to Santa Cruz de Villegas. The clash showed that Mexicans of every faction resented the expedition and led Pershing to pull his columns back north.

sources.citation: Clarence C. Clendenen, Blood on the Border: The United States Army and the Mexican Irregulars (Macmillan, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Battle of Carrizal
properties.label: Carrizal
properties.description: Two troops of the 10th Cavalry under Captain Charles T. Boyd tried to force their way east through the town of Carrizal against the orders of the Carrancista commander, General Félix Gómez. Both commanders were killed, and the Americans lost about a dozen dead and some two dozen captured. The two countries came close to war, and the crisis was settled only by negotiation.

sources.citation: Clarence C. Clendenen, Blood on the Border: The United States Army and the Mexican Irregulars (Macmillan, 1969).
Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).

properties.title: Constitution of 1917
properties.label: Constitution of 1917
properties.description: A Constituent Congress of Carrancista delegates met at Querétaro and, going beyond Carranza's draft, wrote a constitution with radical social articles: Article 27 vested ownership of land, waters and the subsoil in the nation, allowing land reform and asserting control of oil; Article 123 set labour rights; Article 3 made education secular. It was promulgated on 5 February 1917 and is still in force.
properties.note: Marked at the Teatro de la República (then Teatro Iturbide), where the Congress sat.

sources.citation: Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, promulgated at Querétaro, 5 February 1917 (Diario Oficial de la Federación, 5 February 1917).
E. V. Niemeyer Jr., Revolution at Querétaro: The Mexican Constitutional Convention of 1916–1917 (University of Texas Press, 1974).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Zapata assassinated at Chinameca
properties.label: Chinameca
properties.description: Colonel Jesús Guajardo, a Carrancista officer under General Pablo González who pretended to be ready to defect, lured Zapata to the hacienda of Chinameca in southern Morelos, where his troops shot him at the gate. By then González's campaigns had devastated Morelos, but the Zapatista chiefs held out, and in 1920 they joined Obregón.
properties.note: Marked at Chinameca (municipality of Ayala); the hacienda stood in the village.

sources.citation: John Womack Jr., Zapata and the Mexican Revolution (Alfred A. Knopf, 1969).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Plan of Agua Prieta
properties.label: Plan of Agua Prieta
properties.description: When Carranza tried to impose a civilian successor, Ignacio Bonillas, and sent troops into Sonora, the Sonoran leaders under Governor Adolfo de la Huerta and Plutarco Elías Calles disowned him in the Plan of Agua Prieta, backing Obregón. Most of the army joined within weeks, and Carranza abandoned the capital.

sources.citation: Plan de Agua Prieta, 23 April 1920.
Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Carranza killed at Tlaxcalantongo
properties.label: Tlaxcalantongo
properties.description: Carranza left Mexico City by train for Veracruz on 7 May 1920 with his government, the treasury and the archives. When rebel attacks stopped the trains in eastern Puebla, he fled on horseback into the Sierra Norte de Puebla, and in the early hours of 21 May he was shot in a hut at the village of Tlaxcalantongo by troops of Rodolfo Herrero, who had offered to escort him. Adolfo de la Huerta became interim president, and Obregón was elected that autumn.
properties.note: Marked at San Antonio Tlaxcalantongo (municipality of Xicotepec, Puebla). The flight from the trains through the sierra is not drawn because its stages are not securely located.

sources.citation: Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1920, vol. III, doc. 159: the US chargé in Mexico to the Secretary of State, 7 May 1920 (Office of the Historian, US Department of State).
Alan Knight, The Mexican Revolution, 2 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Linda B. Hall, Álvaro Obregón: Power and Revolution in Mexico, 1911–1920 (Texas A&M University Press, 1981).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.

properties.title: Villa surrenders at Sabinas
properties.label: Villa surrenders
properties.description: After a march across the desert of the Bolsón de Mapimí, Villa occupied the coal town of Sabinas, Coahuila, and there signed an agreement with General Eugenio Martínez, acting for interim president de la Huerta. He laid down his arms in exchange for the hacienda of Canutillo, in northern Durango, and an escort of fifty men paid by the government. It ended a decade of revolutionary war, though not of rebellion.
properties.note: Most sources give 28 July 1920; a few give other dates.

sources.citation: Friedrich Katz, The Life and Times of Pancho Villa (Stanford University Press, 1998).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 15.
